# A gate's true positive is the batch's finding, wherever it lies

Status: `open`: the change is crustify `9f42026` on
`libgit2-crustify/evolution/gate-findings-outside-the-workset`, awaiting its review. It touches a protected path, so it
lands only with the user's approval.

## Signal

A rule an agent had to work out by hand that a skill should state. `reviewing`'s Gates
section says only that "without `fix`, each true positive a gate finds is filed as a UB
report"; its Worklists section has a review "report only on" its workset. A gate runs over
the whole workspace, so a true positive it finds may lie outside the workset, and the two
rules then leave it to no one: neither says whether a review under `fix` files it, patches
it, or leaves it.

## Evidence

`wave-229/batch-1/run-1`, the module pass of `src/util/utf8.c`: its module's end gates, TSan
over the workspace on the wave's tip `680ac73bf`, failed the `lib` binary with a data race in
`src/libgit2/filter.c`, far from the module. It reproduced alone, from safe code
(`crustify/reviews/modules/libgit2/src/util/utf8.c/wave-229/batch-1/ub_safe/first-filter-loads-race-on-builtin-filter-flags`,
exit 66 five runs of five), and `filter.rs`'s module docs had named it as open since the
tree was homed. An earlier review of the same race (`legacy-wave-49/batch-1`'s
`misc/matched-path-workdir-tests-race-the-first-filter-load`) had filed it as a test defect
of its fixture, and a later batch (`wave-332`) serialized another fixture around it: each
left the defect to the module that owned it, which no batch revisited. The pass filed it,
patched it (`runtime_pinned` initialises the built-in filters) and turned the reproducer
into a regression test, reasoning that the gate was its own.

## Destination

The spec: `reviewing`'s Gates section, which the reviewer's role evolves.

## Change

crustify `1423c7f`: the section's sentence becomes "Each true positive a gate finds is a
finding of the batch, filed as a UB report and, under `fix`, patched, whether or not the
workset holds the code it reaches: the gate is the batch's, and a report it leaves to no one
is lost."; and its `EVOLUTION.md` entry.

## Record

The row for `EVOLUTION.md`, copied in when the change lands. The change was made as crustify
`1423c7f`, which also edited `EVOLUTION.md`; on 2026-11-14 it was rebased onto the working
branch as `9f42026`, without that edit, since a change's row is drafted in its proposal.

its reproducer, the fix makes the reproducer exit 0 five runs of five, and the regression

be8cb16 EVOLUTION.md: record five binding and porting rules
     1	---
     2	name: reviewing
     3	description: "How landed work is reviewed: tiered review batches and module passes, depth by how long code lasts, worklists, objectives, reports, reproducers, fixes, gates and plan corrections. Read before reviewing a batch, filing a finding or correcting an earlier plan."
     4	---
     5	
     6	# Reviewing
     7	
     8	Review inspects work that has already landed, for a set of objectives, and files a report
     9	for every defect it finds. In a translation campaign, it inspects what each
    10	translation batch landed before the waves that build on it start; in an audit, the modules of a crate
    11	that Crustify did not generate (see [`audit-workflow`](../../workflows/audit-workflow/SKILL.md)); and planner runs review the
    12	plan that earlier runs committed (see [Plan corrections](#9-plan-corrections)).
    13	
    14	## 1. Review batches
    15	
    16	When review is enabled, every translation batch's landing is reviewed before its wave is
    17	promoted, so that no wave builds on unreviewed work. A review batch is a batch of the wave
    18	it reviews, in `schedule.json`, that `reviews` some of its landed translation batches, and
    19	lands on the same integration branch, as [`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)
    20	names it. The wave is promoted
    21	once its translation batches and their reviews have landed. An audit's review waves are
    22	[`audit-workflow`](../../workflows/audit-workflow/SKILL.md)'s.
    23	
    24	Review is tiered. Each landing is reviewed within its wave, to the depth
    25	[Depth](#11-depth) gives it. Before a module's switch in a port, and at its end in a
    26	wrap, a module pass reviews the module whole, across its batches: its unsafe regions, its
    27	exports and its tests. It is the last review batch of the last wave of the module's `wrap`
    28	and `port` items, not of a port's later stages, marked
    29	`module_pass`, launched once every other batch of that wave has landed; its worklist is
    30	the module's paths, and it runs the wave's gates and the module's end gates, as
    31	[Gates](#7-gates) describes. A module whose run landed a single translation batch is
    32	reviewed by its module pass alone, whose workset is that batch's whole: a review of the
    33	batch before it would read the same code twice.
    34	
    35	A review batch also reads the campaign's lessons that are `provisional`, as
    36	[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md)'s Lessons section describes: those its
    37	worklist's commits add or change, and those no worklist holds.
    38	
    39	Review batches are packed eagerly, as the batches they review land: one launches as soon as
    40	the landed batches not yet reviewed fill it, and the last once every translation batch of
    41	the wave has landed, so that review runs beside the wave's remaining batches rather than
    42	after them. When a session runs only part of a wave, or part of the scope, its review
    43	covers what it landed, before what consumes that starts.
    44	
    45	A review batch takes the commits of translation batches of one route, `type` or `symbol`,
    46	counted over their items: types and symbols are reviewed apart. It is larger than a
    47	translation batch, since its reviewer reads landed code rather than writing it, and is
    48	sized as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Batches section sizes one,
    49	from what landed rather than what is planned: its lines, its unsafe sites and raw-pointer
    50	positions, the regions it touches and the objectives it carries, without overwhelming its
    51	reviewer, and within the settings' review caps (`id: review-workload`) when they set them.
    52	A campaign may also review every translation batch on its own, with that batch's commits.
    53	
    54	A review batch's `task.json` holds its worklist, its objectives, its wave branch and its
    55	run fields, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Review batches section
    56	describes. Without `objectives`, a batch runs every objective that applies: those this skill's
    57	Objectives section and the tool skills describe.
    58	
    59	### 1.1 Depth
    60	
    61	How deeply a landing is reviewed follows how long its code lasts, as
    62	[`testing`](../testing/SKILL.md)'s thoroughness does. A wrapper a port will replace, its
    63	item's port planned in `schedule.json`, keeps its safe API through that port: it is
    64	reviewed on its public API, for every objective that applies there, `ergonomics` included,
    65	and not on its internals. An export is reviewed lightly while the C that calls it is
    66	scheduled for porting, and thoroughly once it serves C that stays, for good or when a ship
    67	point releases its module. Everything else is reviewed for every objective that applies.
    68	
    69	## 2. Worklists
    70	
    71	A review batch has one route:
    72	
    73	| route | worklist | workset |
    74	|---|---|---|
    75	| `commits` | commits that translation batches landed | the code they add or change, and what it reaches |
    76	| `paths` | source files and directories of a crate, or named types, trait impls and functions in one | everything they define, or the named parts |
    77	| `reports` | none: the batch only revisits reports | the code the reports name |
    78	
    79	A review batch's entry in `schedule.json` names the batches of its wave it
    80	`reviews`, and each of those lists the `commits` it landed and the `items` it bound or
    81	ported, whose `kind` gives their routes, `type` or `symbol`, as
    82	[`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes section describes.
    83	
    84	A module named with `types`, `trait_impls` or `functions` limits the workset to those: a
    85	type with its fields and its inherent impls, wherever they are; a trait impl, named
    86	`<trait> for <type>` as its header spells it, with its methods and associated items; a
    87	free function with nothing else. What they call and what implements their traits is read,
    88	but only the workset is reported on.
    89	
    90	## 3. Objectives
    91	
    92	Each objective names a kind of defect. A tool may contribute objectives of its own.
    93	
    94	### 3.1 Unsafety (`unsafety`)
    95	
    96	Unsafe annotations and raw pointers on the workset's public API that safe, idiomatic
    97	variants could replace, so that API consumers write less unsafe code.
    98	
    99	### 3.2 Contracts (`contracts`)
   100	
   101	Safety contracts that are incorrect, incomplete or ambiguous:
   102	
   103	- the `# Safety` obligation of a public entry point that must legitimately stay unsafe: a
   104	  caller who honours it can still reach undefined behaviour, or it asks for something the
   105	  implementation does not need;
   106	- the `// SAFETY:` justification of an `unsafe` block: the invariant it claims does not
   107	  hold on every path that reaches the block, or no comment justifies the block at all;
   108	- an obligation stated on code that C calls once a value is handed to it, such as the
   109	  members of a callback table a safe constructor builds for C to install: C, not the Rust
   110	  caller, then chooses the arguments, often from data it reads, so no caller can honour it.
   111	  What the obligation excludes is refused in Rust, in front of the C, instead, where Rust
   112	  can test it, such as a value, a range, a null or a length. One Rust cannot test, such as
   113	  a pointer's liveness or family, or a string's terminator, is kept by whoever hands the
   114	  value to C: the C declaration's own contract, which the code it calls trusts as an
   115	  export does, or an `unsafe` installer whose Rust caller vouches for it. Only an
   116	  obligation neither covers, and Rust can test, is a finding.
   117	
   118	A contract is tested by trying to break it: an input, a call sequence or an interleaving
   119	that honours the obligation, or reaches the block through safe code, and still violates
   120	what the `unsafe` relies on. Contracts are judged by the side of the boundary they serve:
   121	the gateways through which C reaches the crate, its `ffi_export` regions, and every other
   122	unsafe code, which in a Crustify-generated crate sits in its `ffi_import` regions, whose
   123	items are sound for every input their module can give them, as
   124	[`binding`](../../rust/binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section requires.
   125	
   126	### 3.3 UB (`ub`)
   127	
   128	UB in the workset's API that its UB tests missed, by where it is reached from: the safe
   129	public API, the unsafe public API within its `# Safety` obligations, or C through an
   130	export within the C declaration's contract. The unsafe surface includes only the API the
   131	workset adds; a workset that made no API item unsafe has none.
   132	
   133	### 3.4 Equivalence (`equiv`)
   134	
   135	Functional equivalence defects in the workset's API that its equivalence tests missed,
   136	while the C it translates exists: in a port, until the module's switch. A divergence is a defect only when it is unintended: a doc comment, a `CHANGELOG`
   137	entry, a named test asserting the new behaviour or a commit message explaining it marks it
   138	deliberate, and one that corrects a C defect on purpose is no finding.
   139	
   140	### 3.5 Logic (`logic`)
   141	
   142	Behaviour that departs from the library's intended specification, in the workset's public
   143	API or its private implementation, that its tests missed. The specification is, from the
   144	most authoritative: the formats and standards the library implements, its documentation,
   145	what its own test suites assert, and its maintainers' stated intent. A finding cites what
   146	the behaviour departs from. Where the C departs from it too, the defect is not copied into
   147	the Rust, and the finding records the C's. A leak, a deadlock or a panic on valid input
   148	departs from nearly every specification.
   149	
   150	### 3.6 Ergonomics (`ergonomics`)
   151	
   152	Public API that is harder to use than it needs to be: its names, its conversions, its
   153	iterators, builders or defaults where the C takes long argument lists, and the standard
   154	traits its types lack. An item's safe API is fixed by the first batch that gives it one, a
   155	wrap included, so its ergonomics are reviewed there.
   156	
   157	### 3.7 Idiom (`idiom`)
   158	
   159	Ported implementation that transliterates its C rather than using Rust's own means: index
   160	loops where iterators fit, status codes where `Result` and `?` fit, lengths and releases
   161	carried by hand where ownership carries them.
   162	
   163	### 3.8 Conventions (`conventions`)
   164	
   165	Deviations from the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md), in a Crustify-generated
   166	batch only, unsafe code outside its regions included.
   167	
   168	### 3.9 Misc (`misc`)
   169	
   170	Any other defect in the workset.
   171	
   172	### 3.10 Test adequacy (`test-adequacy`)
   173	
   174	Gaps in the workset's tests: the C and Rust execution paths, and the states and
   175	transitions, that the codebase's external and inline test suites leave unreached, found by
   176	reading those suites against the code and measured as
   177	[`testing-builds`](../testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section describes; assertions too
   178	weak to fail when the code is wrong; tests outside the suite of their kind; and the C test
   179	cases none carries over. A gap is filled with tests, not filed: the coverage measurement
   180	shows the delta.
   181	
   182	### 3.11 Revisit (`revisit`)
   183	
   184	The reports an earlier review filed, each rerun through its reproducer on the current
   185	tree. One that still reproduces stays a finding of its objective; one that no longer does
   186	has its report updated with the commit that changed the verdict; one that was never a
   187	defect is removed, with the reason in the commit message.
   188	
   189	### 3.12 Disclosure (`disclose`)
   190	
   191	A `disclosure.md` beside each report that the user can send to the affected project's
   192	maintainers unchanged: under 450 words, following the project's conventions for
   193	disclosing security and UB issues, in an email-friendly format naming the maintainers when
   194	it goes by email first. It includes a small snippet and the sanitizer crash or failing
   195	assertion, offers the reproducer on request, and offers patches only under `fix`. It ends
   196	with: `Found by [Crustify](https://github.com/crustify-rs/crustify), an experimental
   197	UB/soundness auditing agent developed at UC Berkeley and running on <model name>, then
   198	manually reviewed and independently reproduced.`
   199	
   200	### 3.13 Fix (`fix`)
   201	
   202	Whether a review patches what it finds. Without it, a review changes nothing outside
   203	its reviews dir but the tests that fill the gaps `test-adequacy` finds.
   204	
   205	## 4. Reports
   206	
   207	A review batch files its findings under its reviews dir, as
   208	[`layout`](../../operations/layout/SKILL.md)'s Reviews section spells it,
   209	each in its own `<slug>` directory, holding its report and, when it has one, its
   210	reproducer, in the sub-directory of its objective:
   211	
   212	| objective | sub-directory |
   213	|---|---|
   214	| `unsafety` | `unsafe/` |
   215	| `contracts`, of a gateway | `contracts/ffi_export/` |
   216	| `contracts`, of other unsafe code | `contracts/ffi_import/` |
   217	| `ub`, on the safe interface | `ub_safe/` |
   218	| `ub`, on the unsafe interface | `ub_unsafe/` |
   219	| `ub`, through an export | `ub_export/` |
   220	| `equiv` | `equiv/` |
   221	| `logic` | `logic/` |
   222	| `ergonomics` | `ergonomics/` |
   223	| `idiom` | `idiom/` |
   224	| `conventions` | `conventions/` |
   225	| `misc` | `misc/` |
   226	
   227	A tool may add sub-directories for findings on its own output. A defect in a tool
   228	rather than in the reviewed codebase, Crustify included, is no finding: it is a proposal,
   229	with its reproducer, as [`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md)'s Proposals
   230	section describes.
   231	
   232	A report states what is wrong, where, the evidence that proves it, and, under `fix`, how it
   233	was fixed. It names the tier that caught the finding, and the tiers that had the same code
   234	in scope before it and passed it. The tiers are a batch's own gates, a review batch, a
   235	module pass, a switch, a later stage's review, a revisit, a ship point's gates and a
   236	consumer. A finding caught by a later tier than the first that had it in scope is an
   237	escape. A finding that a switch, a ship point's gates or a consumer catches is filed by the

     6	# Evolution
     7	
     8	How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and

    10	campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets

    19	full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
    20	are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

    23	its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the

   140	  its writer did not think to keep.
   141	
   142	The lessons are reconciled at each ship point, and whenever five have been added or changed
   143	since the last pass: duplicates are merged, stale lessons are retired, scopes are checked,
   144	and a lesson that can be stated without the target's names is proposed for the spec, as is
   145	one a second campaign records again, by a proposal citing both. A lesson the pass changes
   146	is `provisional` again.
   147	
   148	## 6. Changes
   149	
   150	A campaign evolves each component, Crustify or a tool, on a working branch of its own in
   151	that component's repository, `<campaign-id>/devel`, the campaign id being the name of the
   152	campaign's repository. It is forked from the component's `devel` when the campaign first
   153	needs it, and the campaign's runs read and run the component from its checkout, so that a
   154	campaign runs on what it has changed and no other campaign does.
   155	
   156	A change is made on a branch named `<campaign-id>/evolution/<slug>`, forked from that
   157	working branch, in a worktree beside the repository that lives only while the change is
   158	made. A branch holds one concern. Once the change lands on the working branch, by a
   159	fast-forward, the worktree is purged and the branch deleted. Its commits take the identity
   160	[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives the
   161	campaign's.
   162	
   163	- A change to the spec follows `authoring`: written once, in the place its kind belongs,
   164	  as generally as the evidence allows.
   165	- A change to what a tool does comes with a regression test: the reproducer of a defect
   166	  becomes one, and a new behaviour gets one that fails without it. A change to its
   167	  documentation alone adds none, unless the defect it fixes has a reproducer, which becomes
   168	  a test or a doctest. A packaging defect's reproducer becomes a test too, run
   169	  against a build installed as a dependent installs it. The tool's whole suite passes, its
   170	  opt-in tests included wherever the change touches what they cover.
   171	- A new tool is drafted and tested where it serves a repeated procedure, preferably as a
   172	  subcommand of an existing tool within that tool's goals, or as a script in the skill
   173	  that describes its use, as `authoring` places one; a tool of its own repository is
   174	  merged upstream only with the user's approval.
   175	
   176	A fix that unblocks the campaign, or that would prevent a defect in later campaigns, is
   177	landed on the working branch as soon as it is reviewed, rather than batched.
   178	
   179	## 7. Validation
   180	
   181	A tool's change is validated by its tests, the regression test it adds among them.
   182	
   183	A spec change that a failure prompted is validated by running again what failed, the item,
   184	the batch or the stage, under the change: a lightweight run, without the tests or gates
   185	the failure does not need to show. The proposal records what the run produced before and
   186	after, and a change whose rerun still fails does not land. A spec change no failure
   187	prompted, such as a rule loosened or a waste removed, is validated the same way where its
   188	effect is in doubt, on the item its evidence came from.
   189	
   190	A rerun shows that a change answers the case that exposed it, not that it holds: that is
   191	watched in the campaigns after it lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes.
   192	
   193	## 8. Review
   194	
   195	Every change is reviewed before it lands, on its evolution branch, by a run other than the
   196	one that made it. A change is finished once its proposal names its commit. A finished
   197	change is reviewed before the next wave of its campaign launches, so that later runs work on
   198	the fix rather than around it. The review reads the proposal, the change and its validation, and checks
   199	that:
   200	
   201	- the proposal's evidence shows the signal, and the change answers it;
   202	- the change serves a goal, and a tool's stays within the tool's own goals;
   203	- it is placed and written as [`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md) describes, and states
   204	  no rule in the target's names;
   205	- its validation was run, and shows what the proposal says;
   206	- the row its proposal drafts for the record, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes, names a recurrence
   207	  signal a campaign would observe, and `test` only where its test checks all of it; and
   208	- whether it weakens a check, which the verdict marks.
   209	
   210	A review runs under the campaign's working branch of the component, never under the change
   211	it reviews, and reads the change from its branch. Its task pins the commit it reviews, and
   212	only that commit lands, by a fast-forward of the working branch: a commit added after the
   213	verdict, or one a rebase or cherry-pick makes, is reviewed again. Its checks are this section's and its
   214	role's; the task message of the run that asks for it adds to them, and never relaxes them.
   215	A review reads as deeply as the change reaches: a change to documentation alone is read; a
   216	tool's code, a check, a soundness fix and every rule of the spec are reviewed with their
   217	validation run again.
   218	
   219	The verdict is recorded in the proposal's Review section, approved or rejected, with its
   220	reasons; a rejection leaves the proposal open for another change or for the user.
   221	
   222	What only records what was decided changes no rule and is not reviewed: a row of the index,
   223	a status of the record, or a proposal's status, verdict and review. A row of the record is
   224	reviewed in its proposal, with its change.
   225	
   226	A change that weakens a check, a gate, a test, a lint, a review objective, a tool's
   227	detection or a rule of this skill, is marked so in the verdict and in its entry of the
   228	record, since a run that can loosen what judges it passes by loosening it: the user reads
   229	each such change on its own before `devel` takes it, as [Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.
   230	
   231	## 9. Autonomy
   232	
   233	The settings' `evolution` answer sets how far a campaign evolves the harness:
   234	
   235	| answer | what lands on the campaign's working branches |
   236	|---|---|
   237	| `off` | nothing: no proposal, no lesson |
   238	| `propose` | nothing but the index's rows and the record's statuses: proposals and lessons are filed, and no rule changes |
   239	| `repair` | each fix of a defect |
   240	| `evolve` | also each improvement and discovery |
   241	
   242	A change lands on its component's working branch as soon as its review approves it, without
   243	the user's approval: the working branch is the campaign's own, and nothing else runs on it.
   244	
   245	The protected paths are the exception. They hold what judges the work, and a run that can
   246	loosen what judges it passes by loosening it. In Crustify's repository they are:
   247	
   248	- `GOALS.md`;
   249	- `skills/crustify/evolution/**` and `skills/verification/**`, the scripts beside those
   250	  skills included;
   251	- `skills/artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md`;
   252	- the Lints and Unsafe code sections of `skills/rust/toolchain/SKILL.md`;
   253	- the Testing, Reviewing and Audit sections of `skills/tools/*/SKILL.md`, and every section
   254	  of one that describes a scan a landing passes, such as `ffimap`'s Binding › Safe boundary;
   255	- `agents/common.md`, `agents/reviewer.md` and the Evolution section of
   256	  `agents/assistant/assistant.md`;
   257	- the `evolution` question of `templates/*/CRUSTIFY.template.md`;
   258	- `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, which decides the skills and hooks a run loads; and
   259	- `providers/generic/compose.py` and, under `providers/claude/`, `compose.py`, `spawn.py`,
   260	  `system-prompt.md`, `hooks.json` and `agents/*.md`. A generated agent that changes only as
   261	  its sources outside this list changed is not a change to a protected path.
   262	
   263	A change whose diff touches a protected path lands on the working branch only with the
   264	user's approval, whatever its review says, and so does the removal of a `weakens a check`
   265	mark from the record. One case lands without that approval: the repair of a defect in
   266	protected code, a script or a provider's program, that blocks the campaign, once its review
   267	approves it and finds three things. The repair weakens no check. Every existing test of the
   268	code it touches is unchanged. The repair adds a regression test of its own. Such a repair is
   269	put to the user at the next module's end. A change to a protected text always waits for the
   270	user. A
   271	change to `GOALS.md` is proposed and never made, unless the user asks for it, since
   272	`GOALS.md` is what every other change is judged against.
   273	
   274	A component's `devel` is the user's gate. It takes a campaign's working branch only with
   275	the user's approval, asked for at each module's end and at the campaign's end, with the
   276	record's entries since the last advance, those the review marked as weakening a check
   277	first. Where `devel` has moved meanwhile, the working branch takes it by merge before it
   278	is offered. What the user declines is reverted on the working branch or stays there, as
   279	they say, and is recorded so; where it weakened a check, what landed under it is reviewed
   280	again, by review batches with `revisit`, as [Adoption](#10-adoption) schedules them for a
   281	soundness fix. Merging a component's `devel` into its `main`, and merging a
   282	new tool upstream, need the user's approval too.
   283	
   284	A run that a defect blocks does not work around it. Where the answer lets fixes land, it
   285	makes the fix on its evolution branch; under `propose` it files the proposal, with its
   286	reproducer, and the user is asked at once whether the fix is to be made; and it ends,
   287	reporting which. The fix is reviewed and lands, and the run is run again, as a failed
   288	batch is.
   289	
   290	## 10. Adoption
   291	
   292	Every run's `task.json` records the revisions of Crustify and the tools it launched
   293	under, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Run fields section
   294	describes. A change that lands on a working branch takes effect as it lands: the runs launched
   295	after it record its revision, and a run under way when it lands, which its recorded
   296	revisions and its landing's date tell, may have followed either. What landed before it
   297	under the old rules stays, unless the change fixes a soundness
   298	defect: then the landings it affects are reviewed again, by a review batch with
   299	`revisit`.
   300	
   301	At each module's end, the campaign's evolution is consolidated: open proposals are landed
   302	as the autonomy allows, the working branches are offered to the user for `devel`, and the
   303	revisit batches a soundness fix or a declined weakening calls for are scheduled. The
   304	lessons are reconciled when [Lessons](#5-lessons) times it, and the record's rows are read
   305	when [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) times it.
   306	
   307	## 11. The record
   308	
   309	The record of what landed, `EVOLUTION.md`, and how evolution itself evolves from it are
   310	[`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s.

Read before drafting a change's row, writing or reading the record, or proposing a change to the evolution protocol."
     4	---
     5	
     6	# Evolution record
     7	
     8	The record of what [`evolution`](../SKILL.md) landed, and what evolution learns from it.
     9	
    10	## 1. Record
    11	
    12	Every change that lands is recorded in Crustify's own repository, in
    13	[`EVOLUTION.md`](../../../../EVOLUTION.md), whatever component it changed, so that a later
    14	campaign can tell whether it held. A row gives the campaign and proposal the change came
    15	from, the component and commit it landed as, the signal it answered, its recurrence signal
    16	and its status, with a change that weakens a check marked so in its status. A change no
    17	proposal filed names its campaign and `no proposal` in its place, with where it came from.
    18	A proposal that lands several changes takes a row for each.
    19	
    20	A change's row is drafted in its proposal, so that the review reads it. The record's writer
    21	copies the row into the record when the change lands. An evolution branch never edits
    22	`EVOLUTION.md`, so that two changes awaiting review never conflict there, and the record
    23	has one writer per campaign. The record holds every change landed since it began, on
    24	2026-11-12; what landed before is not recorded.
    25	
    26	The recurrence signal is what a campaign would observe if the issue were back, in what a
    27	campaign produces anyway: a review finding of a category, a run that fails for a cause, a
    28	tool's error, a correction the user repeats. A change whose regression test checks all of
    29	it has `test` in its place and is not watched. One with no signal a campaign could observe
    30	has `none`, with why, and is not watched either.
    31	
    32	A watched change is:
    33	
    34	- `watched` from its landing;
    35	- `recurred` once its signal is met again, with the evidence, which opens a proposal that
    36	  cites the row: the change was wrong or partial, or the validation and review that passed
    37	  it were; and
    38	- `confirmed` once a campaign other than the one it came from has ended, having exercised
    39	  it, without the signal.
    40	
    41	A row's signal is looked for at two times, in every campaign:
    42	
    43	- when a proposal is indexed, as [`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Proposals section describes:
    44	  a signal that matches a row's recurrence signal marks that row `recurred`; and
    45	- periodically, when the rows still `watched` are read against the findings, failed runs,
    46	  proposals and corrections since the last reading. The campaign sets the period from its
    47	  state, shorter after a change to a check lands or while findings cluster, longer while
    48	  its modules are small: by default, after every fifth module it integrates. The rows are
    49	  always read at each ship point and at an audit's end.
    50	
    51	The record is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign and reaches `devel`
    52	with it. Rows are appended in landing order and statuses edited in place, so that a merge
    53	of two campaigns' working branches keeps both campaigns' rows, ordered by their landing.
    54	Under `propose`, where no rule changes, the readings still run and their statuses are
    55	committed all the same, since a record commit changes no rule, and they are put to the user
    56	with the campaign's proposals. Under `off`, they do not run.
    57	
    58	## 2. Evolving evolution
    59	
    60	Evolution evolves from its own record, as everything else does from a campaign's. At a
    61	campaign's end the record and the campaign's proposals are read for what repeats: changes
    62	that recurred; changes the review rejected or the user declined, by cause; signals a run
    63	met that no proposal answered; how long a blocking defect held its run; and what the
    64	reviews bought for what they cost: per change, the findings each round made that held, those
    65	its author's own validation had already caught, the rounds it took and their cost. How deep
    66	a review reads, and how many rounds a kind of change gets, follow from that evidence, not
    67	from a fixed rule. Each is a
    68	signal of this guidance, as [`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Signals section lists them, and its proposal is on this
    69	skill, on the agents' evolution rules or on what the review checks.
    70	
    71	Such a proposal is validated and reviewed as any other, and is marked as one that changes
    72	what checks the rest, so that the user reads it on its own before `devel` takes it, as
    73	[`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Autonomy section describes.

     2	name: authoring
     3	description: "How Crustify itself is organized: skills, roles, tool skills and the plugin, where each kind of text goes, and the language every text is written in. Read before changing Crustify, filing a proposal or a lesson, or writing a task message for an agent."
     4	---
     5	
     6	# Authoring
     7	
     8	How Crustify is organized: its skills, its agents and the providers that serve them to an
     9	agent host, and where each kind of text lives. The aim is that every rule is written once,
    10	in the one place its kind belongs, so that changing it changes every agent that follows it,
    11	and no two copies drift apart.
    12	
    13	## 1. Layers
    14	
    15	Crustify is text in three layers, with one more per run:
    16	
    17	| layer | where | voice | holds |
    18	|---|---|---|---|
    19	| skills | `skills/<group>/<name>/SKILL.md` | descriptive, third person | what Crustify's artifacts are and how its work is done: workflows, how-tos, conventions, schemas |
    20	| tool skills | `skills/tools/<tool>/SKILL.md` | descriptive, third person | what each tool is, and how it serves each stage |
    21	| agents | `agents/<agent>.md`, with `agents/common.md`, and the assistant's under `agents/assistant/` | instructive, second person | an agent's identity, inputs, what it owns, its steps and what its role changes in the skill index |
    22	| task messages | `task.md` beside a run's `task.json` | instructive | what one run is given: its inputs, and what it needs beyond its role |
    23	
    24	Each artifact's schema, the meaning of its fields, is a skill under `skills/artifacts/`,
    25	and an example of each is given under `templates/`, which the schema cites. The settings,
    26	dashboard and `.gitignore` templates there are what a campaign copies to start. Examples
    27	hold illustrations, not rules.
    28	
    29	The layers are plain Markdown, so that any agent reads them as files. A provider, under
    30	`providers/<host>/`, serves them to one agent host in its own format, as
    31	[Providers](#4-providers) describes; the layers name no host.
    32	
    33	### 1.1 Skills
    34	
    35	A skill describes. It states what an artifact holds, how a decision is made, what a
    36	procedure produces and when each of its steps happens, never what an agent should do, and
    37	never who does a step: which agent owns which step is the agents'. It does not name the
    38	tools that serve it either: a skill reads the same whether or not a tool is installed, so
    39	a statement such as "each unit's lifecycle role is established while planning" belongs in
    40	a skill, and the wavefront command that records it belongs in wavefront's tool skill.
    41	
    42	Skills are grouped by the part of the work they describe: `workflows/`, `planning/`,
    43	`rust/`, `verification/`, `operations/`, `artifacts/`, `tools/` and `crustify/`. A skill's
    44	name is unique across the groups, since agents invoke it by name. Two kinds of skill
    45	describe how work is done. A how-to, such as `binding` or `porting`, describes how one item
    46	is handled. A workflow, under `workflows/`, describes how one kind of campaign proceeds
    47	from its settings to its results: `setup`, which every campaign shares, and one per kind of
    48	campaign (`binding-workflow`, `porting-workflow`, `audit-workflow`). A workflow names the
    49	how-tos and the layout rather than restating them.
    50	
    51	A skill opens with frontmatter that gives its `name` and its `description`. The
    52	description is all an agent sees of the skill before it reads it, so it says what the skill
    53	covers and before which step it is read. A skill stays under about 4,500 tokens, so that a
    54	host that brings an invoked skill back after compacting an agent's context brings it back
    55	whole; one that outgrows that is split at a section that another step needs on its own.
    56	The parts sit in sub-directories of the skill's own, `skills/<group>/<skill>/<part>/SKILL.md`,
    57	each named `<skill>-<part>`, and the skill's own `SKILL.md` keeps what they share: `binding`
    58	and `porting` keep their boundaries, and their `-types` and `-symbols` parts their routes.
    59	
    60	A skill's directory may also hold a script the skill describes, with its tests beside it,
    61	standard library only, so that it runs wherever the skill is read: `usage` holds
    62	`crustify-usage`.
    63	
    64	A skill or an agent says what a step does and which program does it, never the program's
    65	command lines, flags or options, which change with the program: the program's own `--help`
    66	and documentation give them, and the text sends its reader there. A command appears only
    67	where its exact form is what must hold, and a procedure of several commands that must run
    68	exactly so is a script beside its skill, documented by its own `--help`.
    69	
    70	Every skill's sections are numbered. A reference to a section names it, with or without its
    71	number ("testing-builds' Coverage section", "layout § Lifecycle › Waves"), so that a renumbering
    72	never silently points a reference at another section. A skill links another by its
    73	relative path, with the other's name as the link's text.
    74	
    75	### 1.2 Agents
    76	
    77	An agent instructs. Its file holds what is specific to it: its place among the agents, its
    78	inputs, its workflow steps, and the guidelines that apply to one step or stage. Where a step
    79	follows a skill, the agent names the skill's section rather than restating it ("as the
    80	`scheduling` skill's Order section describes"); where a step adds to it, the agent states
    81	only the addition.
    82	
    83	An agent states what it owns by naming the skill sections it carries out ("you create and
    84	purge every level of the `layout` skill's Lifecycle section"), and adds only what the
    85	skills leave to it: the commands it runs, the judgements it makes, the cases it must not
    86	handle itself.
    87	
    88	Every agent's prompt opens with `agents/common.md`: that every commit takes the identity
    89	[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives, that a task
    90	message's instructions take precedence over the rest of the prompt, except where a skill or a
    91	role says a task message adds to a check and never relaxes it, and how skills and
    92	tool skills are read. Every agent sees every skill, with its description:
    93	its host lists them, or, for a host that does not, the provider fills the index of every
    94	skill at common's `<!-- SKILL INDEX -->` marker from the skills' names and descriptions, so
    95	that each description is written once.
    96	
    97	The agent's own file follows, in three sections, every agent alike:
    98	
    99	- `## Role`: who the agent is, its place among the agents, what it owns and what it leaves
   100	  to others;
   101	- `## Workflow`: its steps, each naming the skills it follows. A skill the description
   102	  already sends the agent to before a step needs no mention; a step names a skill where
   103	  only part of it applies to the agent, or where the agent follows it only in some runs;
   104	  and
   105	- `## Inputs`: what its task message names.
   106	
   107	An agent's file names no value of one run: an integration branch or a batch id is "the one
   108	your task message names". `{crustify_root}` stands for the path of Crustify's checkout,
   109	which a provider fills.
   110	
   111	The assistant has one file for every kind of campaign, `agents/assistant/assistant.md`, with a
   112	`<!-- CAMPAIGN ROLE -->` marker at the end of its Role and a `<!-- CAMPAIGN WORKFLOW -->`
   113	marker as its Workflow, which take the campaign kind's file,
   114	`agents/assistant/translate.md` for a port or wrap campaign or `agents/assistant/audit.md`
   115	for an audit: its `### Campaign` section, what the assistant owns in that kind of campaign,
   116	and, after its `<!-- WORKFLOW -->` marker, its steps.
   117	
   118	### 1.3 Tool skills
   119	
   120	A tool is one program an agent reaches for: wavefront, ffimap, ffibox. Each has one skill,
   121	`skills/tools/<tool>/SKILL.md`, written as every skill is, descriptively and without naming
   122	agents. It states what a campaign uses the tool for, where the tool's state sits in a
   123	campaign, and how the tool's output becomes Crustify's artifacts and decisions. How the
   124	tool works, its configuration, tables, commands and what they mean, is its own
   125	documentation's, which the skill cites by document rather than restating, so that the two
   126	never drift; a fact that documentation lacks is added to it, on a branch of the tool's
   127	repository, not to the skill.
   128	
   129	A tool skill opens with what the tool is, which documentation of its own is read in full
   130	before its first use, and what holds in every use of it; one section per stage follows,
   131	each subsection named after the skill section it adds to ("Scheduling › Order"), stating
   132	only what the tool adds there and naming the documents of the tool that stage reads. Its
   133	description names the stages and steps it serves.
   134	
   135	An agent reads a tool's skill before the first step of its work that the skill's
   136	description names, as `agents/common.md` says, and no other skill names a tool: the
   137	description alone brings an agent to the tool, so it names every stage and step the tool
   138	serves. A tool is removed by deleting its skill.
   139	
   140	## 2. Placement
   141	
   142	| text | goes in |
   143	|---|---|
   144	| what an artifact's fields mean | its schema skill under `skills/artifacts/` |
   145	| what an artifact looks like | its example under `templates/` |
   146	| how a kind of work is done, independent of tools | the skill for that work |
   147	| how a kind of campaign proceeds, step by step | its workflow skill under `skills/workflows/`, with the steps every campaign shares in `setup` |
   148	| a convention every agent follows | `conventions` |
   149	| what one agent does, in which steps, and which steps it owns | that agent's file under `agents/` |
   150	| what every agent holds | `agents/common.md` |
   151	| what the assistant does in one kind of campaign | `agents/assistant/<kind>.md` |
   152	| what a tool is, and how it serves each stage | its tool skill |
   153	| how one host is served the layers | its provider under `providers/<host>/` |
   154	| what one run needs beyond its role | its task message, `task.md` |
   155	| what Crustify is for, which every change is judged against | `GOALS.md`, at Crustify's root |

Exit code 2
# Two threads' first filter loads race on a built-in filter's `initialized` flag (TSan)

- **finding**: `ub_safe/first-filter-loads-race-on-builtin-filter-flags`
- **batch**: `wave-229/batch-1/run-1`, the module pass of `libgit2/src/util/utf8.c`. The
  module's end gates found it: TSan over the workspace, on the wave's tip `680ac73bf`, failed
  `lib` with this race (`libgit2::src::libgit2::checkout::unit_tests` staging files while a
  `blob` unit test initialised the filters). It is outside the module's workset, a
  true positive of its gate, filed and fixed here as `reviewing`'s Gates section has a
  gate's true positives handled.
- **items**: the wrappers of every libgit2 routine that loads a filter list internally,
  `fn::git_repository_hashfile` (`RepositoryRef::hash_file`), `fn::git_index_add_bypath`
  (`IndexMut::add_path`), `git_index_add_all` and `git_index_update_all`, checkout and the
  workdir diffs; and `src/libgit2/src/libgit2/filter.rs`'s `initialise_builtin_filters`,
  which closed the race for that module's constructors alone.
- **affected commit**: `680ac73bf` (the wave's tip); the race predates it: `filter.rs`'s
  module docs named it since the tree was homed per translation unit (`324180e8f`).
- **class**: UB reachable from the safe API: a data race in libgit2's C
  (`src/libgit2/filter.c`), between two threads that share no libgit2 object.

## Finding

libgit2 initialises a registered filter the first time a list selects it:
`git_filter_list__load` reads `fdef->initialized` (`filter.c:569`) and `filter_initialize`
writes it (`filter.c:344`), both under the filter registry's *read* lock, which orders
neither against another reader. Two threads whose first loads overlap therefore race on the
flag, whatever repositories they use, and libgit2's threading guide
(`docs/threading.md`) allows two threads to use two repositories at once.

The crate closed this only among `filter.rs`'s own constructors (`FilterList::new`,
`load`, `load_ext`) and the blob writers, each of which calls `initialise_builtin_filters`,
a `Once` that pushes `crlf` and `ident` onto a scratch list before its first load. libgit2's
routines that load a list inside C do not go through it, as `filter.rs`'s module docs said
("libgit2's defect, which only initialising the filters when the runtime is pinned would
close for the whole crate"). Two threads, each with a repository of its own whose
`.gitattributes` selects `crlf`, hashing a file at once through `RepositoryRef::hash_file`,
race, with no `unsafe`.

## Evidence

`src/main.rs` here (`#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`) runs that scenario, the threads meeting at a
`Barrier` before they hash, so that their loads are the process's first. From the
repository root:

```text
CARGO_TARGET_DIR=crustify/tmp/target-repro-tsan crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh tsan \
  run -q --manifest-path crustify/reviews/modules/libgit2/src/util/utf8.c/wave-229/batch-1/ub_safe/first-filter-loads-race-on-builtin-filter-flags/Cargo.toml
```

On `680ac73bf` it exits 66, five runs of five (`run-affected.log`, paths shortened):

```text
WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race
  Read of size 4 at 0x721800000014 by thread T2 (mutexes: read M0):
    #0 git_filter_list__load src/libgit2/filter.c:569
    #1 git_filter_list_load src/libgit2/filter.c:640
    #2 git_repository_hashfile src/libgit2/repository.c:3601
    #3 <RepositoryRef>::hash_file src/libgit2/src/libgit2/repository.rs
  Previous write of size 4 at 0x721800000014 by thread T1 (mutexes: read M0):
    #0 git_filter_list__load src/libgit2/filter.c:344
    #1 git_filter_list_load src/libgit2/filter.c:640
    #2 git_repository_hashfile src/libgit2/repository.c:3601
SUMMARY: ThreadSanitizer: data race src/libgit2/filter.c:569 in git_filter_list__load
```

(`filter.c:344` is `filter_initialize`'s `fdef->initialized = true`, inlined.)

## Fix

`runtime_pinned` (`src/libgit2/src/util/errors.rs`), the `OnceLock` every safe constructor
passes first, calls `initialise_builtin_filters` once libgit2 is initialised and before it
publishes the pinned runtime: the flags are set before any repository exists, and every
later load is ordered after that write by the `OnceLock`, so libgit2 only reads them. The
pinned runtime is never released, so the registry, and its flags, last for the process.
`initialise_builtin_filters` now only looks the two filters up: `git_filter_lookup` runs
`filter_initialize` for a filter not yet initialised, and neither built-in filter has an
`initialize` callback, so pinning allocates nothing. A first version kept the scratch list
the helper built and freed, and pinning then allocated 145 and 192 bytes, which eleven
allocator-tracing `equiv` tests, each run in a fresh child process, saw in their Rust traces
(`buf`, `odb::sys`, `oidarray`, `strarray` and `util::alloc`); with the lookups alone they
pass unchanged. `filter.rs`'s module docs and `initialise_builtin_filters`' say so; its
other callers stay, returning at once. A filter registered later through `git2/sys/filter.h` is still
initialised by its first load, which that header's wrapper must settle, as before.

The reproducer exits 0 on the fix, five runs of five (`run-fixed.log`). It becomes the UB
test `ub_safe::src::libgit2::filter::first_loads_on_two_threads_do_not_race`, run alone in
a child process (`fixture::isolated`) so that its loads are the process's first: it passes
under TSan with the fix, and fails with this race when `runtime_pinned` skips the call.

API stability: no public item changes.

`disclosure.md` beside this report is for libgit2's maintainers: the defect is theirs, and

A cost outlier, and a rule an agent works around. The `evolution` skill's Review section has
"a commit added after the verdict, or one a rebase or cherry-pick makes" reviewed again. A
change lands only by a fast-forward, so each landing moves the tip and every other approved
change must be rebased, which that sentence sends back to review though nothing in it changed.

## Evidence

On 2026-11-14 seven changes were approved on one tip of `libgit2-crustify/devel`. Landing the
first rebased the rest:

- `type-erased-field-tagged-by-a-sibling` and `export-signature-check` were approved as

- A first review of a one-sentence change cost `$1.3` to `$2.0` that day (five cost `$8.36`),
  so reviewing the five again would have cost about what their first reviews did, to read the
  same diffs.
- The user approved landing them as they were, a departure from the rule, asked for each time.

## Destination

The spec: the `evolution` skill's Review section.

## Change

> ... a commit added after the verdict, or one a rebase or cherry-pick makes, is reviewed
> again, unless it is the reviewed commit rebased with its diff unchanged, as `git patch-id`

The second condition keeps the case where another landing changed the text around the
change, which an unchanged diff does not show.

### Soundness

- **Measure.** The defects a reproducer proves, as the review reports file them by kind.
  These defects are undefined behaviour and contracts that can be broken.
- **Paired with** the escapes among these defects.
- **Not taken yet.** The tier that caught a defect. Also the unsafe sites a review read,
  which the defects are counted against.

## 5. Verification

What the agents produce is machine-checked wherever it can be, rather than left to an
agent's judgement. It is checked by types, lints, sanitizers, Miri, schemas, deterministic
tools and compile-time assertions.

- **Measure.** The line coverage of the ported Rust.
- **Paired with** the share of deliberate faults that the ported Rust's tests catch, since
  code that runs is not code that is checked.
- **Paired with** the gate results that a run reported and that its landed tree does not
  reproduce. A review files these gate results among its reports.
- **Not taken yet.**
  - the seeded faults, which are taken only where a review happens to seed them;
  - the region coverage of the ported Rust; and
  - the states and transitions the tests reach.

The user reads this before anything lands. I changed, committed and landed nothing, and created no scratch or build directories.

**Required fix**

- **It contradicts the Reports section (§4) for defects in a tool.** The new sentence says "Each true positive a gate finds is a finding of the batch … and, under `fix`, patched, whether or not the workset holds the code it reaches." But `reviewing` §4 says a defect in a tool, Crustify included, "is no finding: it is a proposal, with its reproducer." End gates run the whole workspace, so a sanitizer report inside ffibox code is a realistic case. The new sentence would then have a reviewer patch the tool inside its batch, skipping the tool's evolution branch, regression test and review. The old sentence had the same "each" but no "whether or not the workset holds…", so it did not invite this as strongly.
  - **Fix:** "Each true positive a gate finds **in the reviewed codebase** is a finding of the batch…". The proposal's row and Change section quote the sentence and would follow.

**What holds**

- **Evidence:** I checked it in the repository and it matches the proposal.
  - The `wave-229/batch-1` report exists, with `run-affected.log` showing the TSan race at `filter.c:569` and `run-fixed.log` showing exit 0.
  - That run's workset was the three `utf8` paths, and it ran with `wave_gates` and `module_pass`, so the patch to `runtime_pinned` in `errors.rs` was outside the workset.
  - The earlier `legacy-wave-49` `misc` report filed the same race as a test defect.
- **Worklists (§2):** no contradiction. Its "only the workset is reported on" covers review reading. The new sentence states its exception outright, so a reader can't miss it.
- **Fixes (§6):** it agrees. The `ub` entry's regression test "on the side of the module it reaches" already fits code outside the workset. §3.13 (`fix`) is unchanged in effect.
- **Checks:** none is weakened. Nothing that was filed before goes unfiled now; the change adds filing under `fix` and widens what gets patched.
- **Writing:** it states no rule in the target's names, sits where it belongs (Gates, which the reviewer evolves), and keeps its reason.
- **Validation:** enough for a one-sentence rule whose effect isn't in doubt. The before case (`legacy-wave-49`, `wave-332` left the defect to its module) and the after case (`wave-229` filed it, patched it and made the reproducer a regression test) are both on record. Rerunning a review under the new text would only repeat what `wave-229` already did. At your instruction I ran no gates and did not rerun the reproducer, so this rests on the recorded logs.
- **Drafted row:** it names a recurrence signal a campaign would observe, and `watched` is right.

**Not required**

- **BSan sentence:** "A BSan report on an earlier wave's items belongs to the last wave's review" is now a special case of the new sentence. It could be deleted, which removes text.
- **Which gates "a gate" covers:** §7 is about the wave's and the module's end gates. Whether a review batch's own regression gates count is left to the reader, although one cited case, `legacy-wave-49`, came from exactly those.
- **"Filed as a UB report":** this wording is older than the change. It doesn't fit a true positive from a plain test run or a lint stage.
- **Duplicate reports:** without `fix`, the same known defect gets filed again at every wave's end, and nothing says to revisit an existing report instead. This is also older than the change.
- **Objectives:** a batch whose task leaves out `ub` is still told to patch a gate's UB under `fix`, while §6 patches only "every finding of the batch's objectives".
- **Recurrence signal wording:** "neither filed nor patched" would read better as "did not file it, or under `fix` did not patch it".
- **Missing goal:** the proposal names no goal or fitness measure, which `evolution` §4 asks for. The change serves Safety › Soundness (defects proved by reproducers) and Verification (gate results filed among the reports). Only 3 of the campaign's 87 proposals name one, so this is a common gap.
- **Wording:** "a report it leaves to no one" reads as if the gate leaves the report. "a finding no batch takes is lost" would be clearer.

I proposed, changed and recorded nothing for evolution. Nothing in this review met a signal that isn't already filed.
